title: Converting a one-car garage into a small machine shop: power, layout, budget
summary: Start with the working envelopes, then locate services and stage the spending.

blocks.heading: A 12 × 20 ft planning sketch
blocks.alt: Top-down garage sketch: delivery door at the bottom; lathe on the left, mill on the right, bench and electrical panel near the top; a central route connects the door and bench. Dashed regions mark machine operating envelopes.
blocks.caption: Fictional room and compact machines. Scale is approximate. Dashed envelopes are assumptions to replace with manufacturer dimensions, not certified clearances.

blocks.heading: Draw the moving machine, not just its base
blocks.body: A 4 ft machine can consume much more than 4 ft of room. Include the mill table at both travel limits, handwheel access, the lathe’s stock and chuck hazards, service doors and a place for the operator. Then keep a route from the entry to every normal work position.

blocks.heading: Where things go in this example
rows: Actual stock length, guarded stock support, chip direction and service access
Right wall, clear of the central route
Full table travel, handle sweep, headroom and lift path
Keep inspection away from coolant spray and grinding grit
Maintain the working space and access required for the actual installation
Near the delivery door, outside the route
Anchor and restrain stored material; do not obstruct door motion
blocks.caption: The sketch reserves zones. It does not establish building-code compliance or machine-specific guarding.

blocks.heading: Walk a part through the room
blocks.body: Bring a length of stock from the door to the rack, then to the lathe, then to the bench. Repeat with the largest planned part and an empty cart. If the route crosses an operating envelope, change the layout or define a stopped-machine transfer procedure before anchoring anything.

blocks.heading: Give the electrician a load list, not a guessed feeder size
rows: Voltage, phase, nameplate rating, starting requirements, intended simultaneous use
Receptacle and local disconnect arrangement per equipment and installation requirements
A machine fault should not leave the room dark
Ratings, duty cycle and startup behavior
Noise, heat, dust and service access
Tool list and likely simultaneous loads
Keep leads out of aisles and away from moving machinery
blocks.caption: Feeder, overcurrent protection, grounding, required protection and permits are design decisions for a qualified installer under local requirements.

blocks.heading: The nameplate is the start of the conversation
blocks.body: A motor’s operating current is not the whole installation calculation. Starting behavior, existing service capacity, multiple loads and equipment instructions matter. A 60 A panel label does not prove a 60 A feeder is needed or available. Leave capacity unresolved until the actual machines and site are known.

blocks.heading: An illustrative $6,000 conversion envelope
rows: Written scope after site and load review
Check shadows at real work positions
Confirm machine weights, delivery path and floor suitability
Chip / fluid control and initial safety provisions
blocks.caption: Planning assumptions, not quotes. Existing lathe and mill are assumed owned. Machine purchases, structural repairs, major service upgrades and ongoing tooling are excluded.

blocks.heading: Commit in the order that preserves options
items: Measure the room, doors, panel area and machine envelopes; mark them with tape.
Review the floor, moving plan, electrical scope, noise and ventilation before accepting delivery.
Revise the drawing against real quotes. Defer a machine if its operating envelope or services do not fit.
Install the approved services, place and secure equipment, then verify access with the room fully stocked.
Make and inspect one modest part. Record the lighting, handling and storage problems it exposes.

items.label: Entry and exit stay clear
items.detail: Test with the door open and closed and a cart parked where it will actually live.

items.label: Operating envelopes do not silently become storage
items.detail: Keep the dashed zones free while machines are in use.

items.label: Panel and service access remain available
items.detail: Confirm the real clearances with the installer and equipment documents.

items.label: Workholding and stock handling have space
items.detail: A tidy empty room is not the same as a usable working room.

items.label: The budget includes a hold point
items.detail: An unpriced power upgrade stops the purchase decision rather than disappearing into contingency.

blocks.heading: Keep incompatible processes apart
blocks.body: This plan is for a small metalworking room. Do not add welding, wood dust or flammable finishing just because a corner looks empty; each changes ventilation, fire and separation needs. A new process deserves another layout review.
